title: The fingers will testify
hook: the Prophet ﷺ counted praises on his fingers, saying they'd be asked and made to speak (Tirmidhi)

segments.voice: Yesterday: fajr, takbir to taslim. Your line was the whole thing. Did you catch the gray sky at dawn? Day one hundred thirteen.

A man sits after the prayer is done. His right hand rests on his knee, palm up. His thumb moves slowly from one finger joint to the next, and his lips move without sound. He isn't fidgeting. He's counting. The same hand, earlier in the day, typed, scrolled, held a cup, maybe tapped a car horn harder than it needed to. Now it's keeping a different kind of record. And the reason for counting this way, on the fingers, is a little startling. Today: the fingers will testify.
screen: `A THUMB MOVING JOINT TO JOINT.` → `HE'S COUNTING.` → `A DIFFERENT KIND OF RECORD.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the prayer. This week opens what comes after it: dhikr, remembrance, the short phrases repeated after the prayer and through the day. And it starts with how they're counted. A hadith in the collection of at-Tirmidhi comes from a woman named Yusayrah, one of the early emigrants. She said the Prophet ﷺ told the women: hold on to glorifying God, and declaring His oneness and holiness, and count on your fingertips, for they will be asked, and made to speak. And don't be heedless, or you'll forget mercy. Asked and made to speak. It echoes the Qur'an. In Surah Ya Sin, it describes the Day of Judgment: mouths are sealed, and hands speak, and feet bear witness to what they earned. Read alone, it sounds like a warning: the body will tell what it did. Set beside this hadith, it can be heard another way. If the fingers will testify anyway, give them something good to say. Let them have counted glory. Another companion, Abdullah ibn Amr, said he saw the Prophet count his praises on his right hand. A common way today is the thumb touching each joint in turn, three on each finger, fifteen on one hand. Prayer beads are used too, and scholars have discussed them, but the reports themselves speak of fingers. Fingers are always with you. You can't leave them at home. And in the hadith's picture, the fingers that counted will one day speak of it.
screen: `THIS WEEK: DHIKR, REMEMBRANCE.` · `COUNT ON YOUR FINGERTIPS.` · `ASKED, AND MADE TO SPEAK.` · `GIVE THEM SOMETHING GOOD TO SAY.` · then, large: `THEY'RE ALWAYS WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count ten on your right hand. Rest the hand, palm up. With your thumb, touch the lowest joint of your little finger. One. The middle joint. Two. The tip. Three. Then the ring finger, three more. Then the middle finger. Keep going until you reach ten. If you pray, you can say a short phrase of remembrance on each count, like subhanallah. If not, just say the numbers, slowly, and feel each joint. Then let the hand rest open. The bell holds the time.
The fingers will testify. Count your praises on your fingertips, the Prophet said, for they'll be asked and made to speak. Today's word.
Your line: the fingers remember. Once today, when your hand reaches for your phone for no reason, touch three finger joints instead, and count. Day one hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: After the prayer and through the day, many Muslims count short phrases of remembrance on the joints of the fingers of the right hand, following the Prophet's example; others use prayer beads.

myth: the Prophet ﷺ counted his praises on prayer beads
the reports speak of his hand; Abdullah ibn Amr saw him count on his right.
a hadith says the fingers will be asked and made to speak
the Qur'an pictures hands speaking on the Day of Judgment
Surah Ya Sin: mouths are sealed, hands speak, and feet bear witness.

fork.setup: you want to keep count of your remembrance after the prayer. what did the Prophet ﷺ tell the women to use?
fork.reveal: count on your fingertips, for they will be asked and made to speak (Tirmidhi, from Yusayrah).

original.note: Arabic: fingertips, the word in the hadith: count on the fingertips.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims count on their fingers to keep track.
what it means: in the hadith, the fingers will testify, so counting praise on them gives them something good to say.
what a scholar hears: Yusayrah's hadith (Tirmidhi 3583) echoing Ya Sin 36:65; Abdullah ibn Amr's report of the right hand (Abu Dawud 1502).

sources.ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3583 (Yusayrah: count on your fingertips, for they will be asked and made to speak)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1502 (Abdullah ibn Amr: counting tasbih on the right hand)
Qur'an 36:65 (mouths sealed, hands speak, feet bear witness)

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook rewritten to open on the scene (was 'Look at your hands... Think about... Now picture'); 'that comes from the Qur'an' softened to 'it echoes the Qur'an'; the 'turns it around' reading framed as one way to hear it; cut 'most scholars count beads as fine', 'the fingers were first' and 'a witness in your favor' (not in the cited texts); myth 3, which tested an interpretation, replaced with a fact from 36:65.
Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm. Yusayrah's hadith is graded hasan or similar by some, weaker by others.
'On his right hand' appears in some narrations of Abu Dawud 1502; please confirm the wording.
Prayer beads (subha, misbaha): most scholars permit; some prefer fingers. Stated as 'most scholars count them as fine'.
The finger-joint method (three per finger) is widespread practice, not stated in the hadith; presented as what many Muslims do.
